claims.text: In-situ substrate pre-heating during additive manufacturing reduces thermal gradients.
Reduced thermal gradients lower residual stress in additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components.
In-situ substrate pre-heating reduces fabrication-induced defects.
In-situ substrate pre-heating improves the dimensional precision of additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components relative to room-temperature-substrate builds.
In-situ substrate pre-heating improves the mechanical integrity of additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components relative to room-temperature-substrate builds.
High-entropy-alloy components additively manufactured on room-temperature substrates typically exhibit high thermal gradients.
High-entropy-alloy components additively manufactured on room-temperature substrates typically exhibit residual stresses and microstructural defects.
Lower thermal gradients produce more uniform solidification.
Lower residual stress and more uniform solidification promote refined microstructural evolution.
Lower residual stress and more uniform solidification minimize porosity and microcracking.
Substrate pre-heating decreases the temperature difference between the incoming melt pool and the underlying material.
Decreasing the melt-pool-to-substrate temperature difference reduces rapid cooling and shrinkage.
Rapid cooling and shrinkage cause residual stresses and defects.
The effectiveness of substrate pre-heating may be limited when temperature cannot be controlled uniformly.
The effectiveness of substrate pre-heating may depend on alloy composition and conventional laser-processing parameters.
